newsitem.title: CHINA: China cities celebrate Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: China cities celebrate Hong Kong handover.

text.p: The final countdown to the recovery of Hong Kong has been a powerful magnet, attracting people from around China to the nation's capital to usher in the start of a new and post-colonial era.
For the tens of millions who could not make it to Beijing, there was the chance to take part in an orgy of celebrations to mark Hong Kong's handover at midnight.
A cavalcade of hundreds of motorcycles drove through the streets of Zhengzhou in the central province of Henan and in the northernmost county of Mohe bonfires were lit along the border with Russia.
A choir of 10,000 lined the banks of Shanghai's Huangpu river and sang the revolutionary hymn "Without the Communist Party there would be no New China" and a new pop song "1997".
In the boomtown of Shenzhen, lion dancers, children beating drums and flag-waving residents cheered as the first 509 active troops of the People's Liberation Army entered Hong Kong.
The heart of the show was in Beijing where 100,000 guests invited to the official party in Tiananmen Square watched a huge digital clock count down the final minutes of British rule over Hong Kong.

Singers belted out saccharine pop songs and children in silk costumes pranced on a huge stage dominating the centre of Tiananmen Square in front of the mausoleum of Chairman Mao Zedong and on the spot where in 1989 troops crushed student-led demonstrations for more democracy.

Jugglers and acrobats performed while dancers dressed in a rainbow of different coloured silks twirled to Chinese songs, including "Beijing Wishes You (Hong Kong) Good Fortune" before the crowd sat on the ground to watch a live broadcast of the handover ceremony from Hong Kong on giant screens.

"It's like a child coming back to the family," said Ma Xun, a 28-year-old car part factory worker."It's a very good show but this kind of organised event can never compare with spontaneous activities by ordinary people."

From remote corners of China many made their pilgrimage, enduring long hours of bumpy bus rides or hard-seat overnight trains to glimpse the gala celebration in Beijing marking the end of more than 150 years of British rule over Hong Kong.

Many were visibly disappointed when unarmed police and paramilitary forces cleared the throngs of visitors from the capital's central Tiananmen Square on Monday afternoon to prepare for the official celebrations.
"I'm disappointed," said one man as he left the square with his friends ahead of the advancing ranks of police and street sweepers.
"We came all the way from Nanjing to see this," he said.

Nanjing, an eastern city now just few hours by train from Shanghai, was where China and Britain agreed in 1842 on the terms that ended the Opium War, including the cession of Hong Kong as a British colony.

China has loudly proclaimed the recovery of the territory as marking an end to its national humiliation at the hands of Western imperial powers. State media have fed the public with a steady diet of news and propaganda on the British colony's return at the stroke of midnight on Monday.
